brief: Goldman Sachs compiles FOMC speakers' public comments since the July meeting, at which the Committee held rates and some members dissented. Three threads run through it. First, most participants condition the September decision on incoming inflation data. Barr would take more time if inflation is moderating toward 2 percent and would act decisively to raise rates if it is not, and Waller would hold if August inflation shows progress but would consider a hike if it comes in hot, while Hammack, Schmid and Musalem argue policy is not restrictive and that tightening is already warranted. Second, on the inflation outlook, Warsh says better than expected summer PCE and CPI readings do not show improved underlying trends and Schmid sees breadth across goods and services, against Waller and Williams who see early disinflation with tariff effects largely passed through. Goldman notes those disinflation comments came before this week's warmer CPI print. Third, almost all participants called the labor market quite stable and consistent with full employment, commenting after a weaker July jobs report but before a stronger August one. The note compiles quotes and states no Goldman house forecast.

cards.claim: Goldman Sachs reports that many FOMC participants have said their view on the appropriate policy stance will depend on incoming inflation data.
cards.anchor: about the appropriate stance of policy will depend on incoming information about inflation.

cards.claim: Goldman Sachs reports that a few FOMC participants share President Hammack's view that policy is not restrictive and that it is time to raise the fed funds rate.
cards.anchor: A few participants, however, have shared President Hammack’s view that “policy is not restrictive”

cards.claim: Goldman Sachs reports that a few FOMC participants agree with Governor Waller that recent data show some signs of disinflation.
cards.anchor: A few others, however, have agreed with Governor Waller who said that “recent data suggest we are finally seeing some signs of disinflation,”

cards.claim: Goldman Sachs notes that the disinflation comments from Waller and Williams were made before this week's warmer CPI print.
cards.anchor: though their comments came prior to this week’s warmer CPI print

cards.claim: Goldman Sachs reports that almost all FOMC participants characterized the labor market in Chairman Warsh's words as quite stable, commenting after a weaker July jobs report but before a stronger August report.
cards.anchor: weaker July jobs report but before a stronger August report—have characterized it, in Chairman Warsh’s words, as “quite stable”

cards.claim: President Hammack said on Sep 4 that both hard data and anecdotes tell her policy is not restrictive.
cards.anchor: Both the hard data and the anecdotes are telling me the same thing: policy is not restrictive.

cards.claim: President Hammack said on Sep 4 that what she is hearing is that it is time to act on rates.
cards.anchor: Right now, what I’m hearing is that it is time to act.

cards.claim: Governor Waller said on Sep 3 he would be inclined to support holding the fed funds target at its current setting if disinflation continues in the data due over the following two weeks.
cards.anchor: I would be inclined to support holding the target for the federal funds rate at its current setting.

cards.claim: Governor Waller said on Sep 3 that he would consider a rate hike if August inflation comes in hot.
cards.anchor: But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.

cards.claim: Governor Waller judges that current policy is only slightly restricting aggregate demand, so it may not take much inflation acceleration to move him toward tighter policy.
cards.anchor: I judge that policy is currently only slightly restricting aggregate demand

cards.claim: President Williams said on Sep 2 that he supported the July FOMC decision not to raise rates and that rates were in a good place to balance the two sides of the mandate.
cards.anchor: I obviously supported our decision not to raise rates at the July FOMC meeting

cards.claim: President Williams said on Sep 2 that recent data have been encouraging but that the Fed has to wait and see rather than judge on a month or two.
cards.anchor: I think we have to wait and see… I would say that the data recently have been encouraging

cards.claim: Governor Barr said on Sep 1 that if data give him confidence inflation is moderating toward 2 percent, the Fed can take more time to assess its policy stance.
cards.anchor: if trends in the data give me some confidence that inflation is moderating on a path to 2 percent

cards.claim: Governor Barr said on Sep 1 that if inflation appears not to be moderating sufficiently, the Fed should act decisively to raise rates.
cards.anchor: if inflation appears not to be moderating sufficiently, then I think we should act decisively to raise rates.

cards.claim: President Goolsbee said on Aug 28 he was personally comfortable holding rates unchanged at the July FOMC meeting.
cards.anchor: I was personally comfortable with holding rates unchanged

cards.claim: President Schmid said on Aug 27 that policy rates might be accommodative on the short end and that the Fed has work to do.
cards.anchor: I think [policy rates] might be accommodative on the short end

cards.claim: President Schmid said on Aug 27 that he would put himself in the camp of the colleagues who dissented at the July FOMC meeting.
cards.anchor: so I would probably put myself in that camp

cards.claim: President Collins said on Aug 25 that the current mildly restrictive stance leaves the Committee well positioned to return inflation to target in a reasonable amount of time.
cards.anchor: this mildly restrictive policy stance should leave the Committee well positioned to address evolving economic conditions

cards.claim: President Collins said on Aug 25 that if sustained inflation progress does not materialize it will be appropriate to tighten policy soon.
cards.anchor: Should evidence of sustained inflation progress not materialize, I believe it will be appropriate to tighten policy soon

cards.claim: President Kashkari said on Aug 23 that he is not confident inflation is heading back down to target in a short period of time.
cards.anchor: feeling confident right now that inflation is heading back down to target in a short period of time.

cards.claim: President Daly said on Aug 20 that she was very supportive of the July hold and that recent inflation and labor market prints did not change her picture.
cards.anchor: The recent prints on both inflation and the labor market didn’t really change that picture for me.

cards.claim: President Musalem said on Aug 20 that monetary policy is neutral or accommodative and that broader financial conditions are pretty accommodative.
cards.anchor: My sense is that monetary policy is neutral or accommodative

cards.claim: President Musalem said on Aug 20 that he was in favor of raising rates at the July FOMC meeting.
cards.anchor: At the July FOMC meeting, I was in favor of raising rates.

cards.claim: President Musalem said earlier and more gradual rate increases are preferable to later, potentially larger and more abrupt increases.
cards.anchor: earlier, more gradual interest rate increases are preferable, better, less disruptive, than later, potentially larger and more abrupt increases

cards.claim: Governor Cook said on Aug 5 that she is prepared to act if she does not see signs of continued disinflation soon.
cards.anchor: If I do not see signs of continued disinflation soon, I am prepared to act.

cards.claim: Governor Cook said five years of above-target inflation raise the risk that higher inflation becomes entrenched in price and wage setting behavior.
cards.anchor: With five years of above-target inflation, the risk grows that higher inflation may become entrenched

cards.claim: President Paulson said on Aug 4 that she sees two plausible scenarios for how current policy is affecting inflation and that incoming evidence will clarify which path the economy is on.
cards.anchor: I see two plausible scenarios for how current policy is affecting inflation

cards.claim: President Paulson said one possibility is that the current fed funds setting is not restrictive enough to deliver 2 percent inflation.
cards.anchor: current policy is not restrictive enough to deliver our target rate of 2 percent inflation.

cards.claim: President Schmid said on Aug 4 that bringing inflation down to the Fed's 2 percent objective will require tighter policy.
cards.anchor: I believe that bringing inflation down to the Fed’s 2 percent objective will require tighter policy.

cards.claim: President Schmid said on Aug 4 that with the labor market in balance and growth resilient his primary concern is inflation.
cards.anchor: With the labor market in balance and growth resilient, my primary concern is inflation.

cards.claim: President Kashkari said on July 31 that he would rather tighten policy incrementally through a potential series of small moves than wait and need bolder action later.
cards.anchor: I would rather tighten policy incrementally as we gather more data on the path of inflation and employment

cards.claim: President Logan said on July 31 that without any policy restraint inflation will likely continue to trend above target until an unanticipated shock.
cards.anchor: Without any policy restraint, inflation will likely continue to trend above target

cards.claim: President Logan said modest action in the near term would reduce the likelihood of needing sharper action later.
cards.anchor: Modest action in the near term would reduce the likelihood of needing to take sharper action later.

cards.claim: President Hammack said on July 31 that she is not confident inflation will return to the Fed's objective on its own.
cards.anchor: I am not confident it will return to our objective on its own.

cards.claim: President Hammack said she sees inflationary pressures coming from the demand side of the economy as well as from supply-side factors including energy prices.
cards.anchor: I see inflationary pressures coming from the demand side of the economy, as well.

cards.claim: President Kashkari said he increasingly believes monetary policy has an important role in addressing a series of successive supply shocks that might entrench higher inflation.
cards.anchor: monetary policy does have an important role to play in addressing a series of successive supply shocks

cards.claim: Chairman Warsh said on Aug 28 that this summer's PCE and CPI readings were better than expected but do not show meaningfully improved underlying trends.
cards.anchor: While this summer’s PCE and CPI readings were better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.

cards.claim: Chairman Warsh said on Aug 28 that the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices.
cards.anchor: So the Fed’s predominant focus right now should be on prices.

cards.claim: President Schmid said measures of inflation that exclude energy are still running solidly above 2 percent.
cards.anchor: Measures of inflation that exclude energy are still running solidly above 2 percent

cards.claim: President Schmid said inflation has been too high across a broad-based and growing cross-section of goods and services.
cards.anchor: Inflation has been too high across a broad-based and growing cross-section of goods and services

cards.claim: President Schmid said the most recent inflation data for June showed an encouraging deceleration but that it would be premature to weight a single data point against recent trends.
cards.anchor: the most recent inflation data for June showed an encouraging deceleration

cards.claim: President Schmid said inflation shocks are not intrinsically transitory and that persistence depends on how the Fed reacts or is expected to react.
cards.anchor: Inflation shocks are not intrinsically transitory.

cards.claim: Governor Waller said on Sep 3 that he does not see elevated energy prices and tariffs as a significant source of ongoing inflation pressure.
cards.anchor: I don’t see elevated energy prices and tariffs now as a significant source of ongoing inflation pressure

cards.claim: Governor Waller said the price effects of tariffs have largely passed through inflation.
cards.anchor: The evidence is that the price effects of tariffs have largely passed through inflation

cards.claim: Governor Waller said nonmarket services prices accounted for approximately half of the increase in core prices in the last PCE report.
cards.anchor: nonmarket services prices accounted for approximately half of the increase in core prices

cards.claim: Governor Waller said that ignoring imputed nonmarket services prices, underlying inflation is doing better than the core numbers suggest.
cards.anchor: my take is that underlying inflation is doing better than the core numbers suggest

cards.claim: Governor Waller said energy prices have moved up again and remain significantly higher than at the beginning of 2026, an upside risk to inflation.
cards.anchor: Energy prices have moved up again and remain significantly higher than they were at the beginning of 2026

cards.claim: Governor Waller said the economy faces pressure on technology goods prices related to the AI buildout.
cards.anchor: the economy faces both pressure on technology goods prices related to the AI buildout

cards.claim: Governor Waller said wage growth net of productivity growth is broadly consistent with inflation continuing to come down to 2 percent.
cards.anchor: wage growth, once one accounts for productivity growth, is broadly consistent with an expectation that inflation is continuing to come down to 2 percent

cards.claim: President Williams said on Sep 2 that he sees neither second-round effects or broadening of tariffs nor unusual broadening of the effects of higher energy prices, and that inflation expectations are well anchored.
cards.anchor: We are neither seeing second-round effects or broadening of the tariffs, nor unusual broadening of the effects of higher energy prices

cards.claim: President Williams said he sees trend inflation moving slowly down as tariff effects move into the rear-view mirror.
cards.anchor: I’m seeing trend inflation moving slowly down as some of the effects of tariffs move into the rear-view mirror.

cards.claim: Governor Barr said a series of shocks from tariffs, the Middle East conflict and the rapid AI buildout pushed the Fed off course.
cards.anchor: A series of shocks—from tariffs and then the conflict in the Middle East, as well as from the rapid AI buildout—pushed us off course.

cards.claim: Governor Barr said core non-housing services inflation remains elevated and that he is closely watching the risk of broader price pressures taking hold.
cards.anchor: core non-housing services inflation remains elevated

cards.claim: President Goolsbee said on Aug 28 that a couple of months of more benign inflation readings do not feel like the Fed is out of the woods.
cards.anchor: that certainly doesn’t feel like we’re out of the woods

cards.claim: President Goolsbee framed the open question as whether inflation is temporary because of the shocks or more persistent because the economy is running hotter than capacity.
cards.anchor: is inflation going to be temporary because of the shocks or is this more persistent

cards.claim: President Collins said the June and July inflation reports were mildly encouraging but that monthly readings can be volatile.
cards.anchor: While June and July inflation reports were mildly encouraging, monthly readings can be volatile.

cards.claim: President Collins said her modal inflation outlook for the rest of 2026 is predicated on limited additional tariff increases and some degree of reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
cards.anchor: This outlook is predicated on seeing limited additional tariff increases and some degree of reopening of the Strait of Hormuz

cards.claim: President Collins said three factors should help gradual disinflation: a balanced labor market, mildly restrictive policy and solid productivity growth.
cards.anchor: I see three factors that should help with the gradual disinflation process

cards.claim: President Collins said there are upside risks to inflation from additional adverse supply shocks and a stronger than expected pace of economic activity.
cards.anchor: there are upside risks to inflation from both additional adverse supply shocks, and a stronger-than-expected pace of economic activity.

cards.claim: President Musalem said persistent demand forces including the AI buildout are one of two reasons inflation is high, working through capex directly and through equity prices and wealth effects indirectly.
cards.anchor: persistent demand forces in the economy, for instance the AI buildout

cards.claim: President Musalem said the US might have another supply shock in the fall with El Nino coming.
cards.anchor: we might have another supply shock in the fall with El Niño coming

cards.claim: President Musalem said inflation stripped of supply shock effects is between 2.5 and 3 percent, which is too high.
cards.anchor: Inflation, when you strip out the effect of supply shocks, is between 2.5 and 3 percent, which is too high.

cards.claim: President Musalem said inflation needs to be brought back down to 2 percent over the next 18 months.
cards.anchor: We need to bring inflation back down to 2 percent over the next 18 months.

cards.claim: Governor Cook said on Aug 5 that her assessment is simple, inflation is too high, and that it has moved significantly away from target over the past year.
cards.anchor: inflation has moved significantly away from our target over the past year

cards.claim: Governor Cook said some disinflationary forces already in play could push inflation toward target without a rate increase.
cards.anchor: Some disinflationary forces are already in play, which could push inflation toward our target without a rate increase

cards.claim: Governor Cook said the price level effects of the tariffs announced last year are mostly behind us.
cards.anchor: the effects of tariffs announced last year on the price level are mostly behind us

cards.claim: Governor Cook cited many forecasters suggesting oil prices, elevated because of the Middle East conflict, will come down by the end of the year and provide deflationary relief.
cards.anchor: many forecasters suggest that they will come down by the end of the year, providing some deflationary relief

cards.claim: Governor Cook said she believes some of the inflationary pressure from the AI buildout will ease as supply chains adjust and sector-specific efficiency gains accrue.
cards.anchor: I believe some of the inflationary pressure coming from the AI buildout will ease

cards.claim: President Paulson said oil prices have jumped and remain volatile, but that the brief period of Middle East stability showed supply shocks can be temporary and reinforces looking through them.
cards.anchor: Oil prices have since jumped and remain volatile, but the brief period of Middle East stability demonstrated that supply shocks can be temporary

cards.claim: President Paulson said the recent improvement in some inflation data is a step in the right direction but only one step.
cards.anchor: It is a step in the right direction, but it is only one step.
